Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.

to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-

sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.

formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome

oral-bioavailability outcome.

records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Direct human absolute/systemic availability measurements for lipophilic basic amines with two aromatic rings and propylamine-type linkers—diphenhydramine (0.69), imipramine-N-oxide (~100%), urapidil (72–78%), donepezil (~100%), laquinimod (high), oxcarbazepine (89%), tiracizine (34%), moexipril (22%), and FK788 (55%)—support F ≥ 20% for the query.

L4 intestinal absorption and permeability records for close structural analogs are strongly supportive: imipramine is essentially 100% absorbed in humans (Fa 100%), desipramine is classified as intestinally absorbed and is a high-permeability internal standard (Caco-2 Papp 82.8×10^-6 cm/s; MDCKII 38.3×10^-6 cm/s), and amitriptyline, pheniramine, and diphenhydramine show high Caco-2 permeability.

L5 gut-wall efflux records do not provide affirmative evidence for F < 20%: desipramine shows high permeability (C182); imipramine has high Papp with efflux ratio ~1.1 in classic Caco-2 and remains highly permeable even when FaSSIF gives an efflux ratio of 2.0 (C214, C178, C180, C211, C192, C195); amitriptyline shows no marked net efflux in rat intestine (C205, C190, C225, C188); methadone is a P-gp substrate yet P-gp inhibitors did not change its bioavailability (C210); dexamphetamine shows efflux ratio 1.2 (C221, C209, C217); asimadoline shows ≥20% absorption within 1 h in both wild-type and P-gp knockout mice (C203).

Low-F records for benazeprilat (<7%, dog 2.57%, cat 3.2%) and FK788 in rat (9.6%) come from polar acids/zwitterions or species-specific contexts and are not transferable to the lipophilic basic diamine query.

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement exists for the query molecule; all support is transferred from structurally related basic amines.
L3 oral AUC/Cmax records lack IV comparators, so they confirm exposure but not the F fraction.
No direct first-pass metabolism or gut-wall metabolism data for the query; F depends on both absorption and first-pass extraction.
The query is predicted to be fully ionized (dicationic) at physiological pH; no direct permeability or efflux measurement quantifies the impact of the second positive charge.
No context exactly matches the N-phenyl-N-indanyl propylenediamine scaffold.
